options.text: `String` owns a heap allocation, so two owners would both try to free it.
`String` is larger, and Rust only copies small types.
options.why_wrong: Size is not the rule. A `[u8; 4096]` is `Copy` and far bigger than a `String`, which is three words on the stack. What matters is whether the type owns a resource.

options.text: `String` is heap-allocated and heap values can never be copied.
options.why_wrong: They can - that is what `.clone()` does. The point is that Rust will not do it implicitly, because it costs an allocation and a memcpy.

options.text: `Copy` only applies to primitive types built into the language.
options.why_wrong: Any type can derive `Copy` if all of its fields are `Copy`. Your own structs can be `Copy`; `String` cannot, because of what it owns.

explanation: `Copy` means duplicating the bits is a complete, correct duplicate of the value. That holds for an `i32`. For a `String` the bits are a pointer, a length, and a capacity - duplicating them gives you two owners of one allocation, and two frees. The rule is about ownership of a resource, not about size.
